title: Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies
author: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras
summary:
Built to Last grew out of a six-year research project at Stanford in which Jim Collins and Jerry Porras compared 18 "visionary companies" (like 3M, American Express, Boeing, Disney, GE, Hewlett-Packard, IBM, Johnson & Johnson, Merck, Nordstrom, Procter & Gamble, Sony, and Walmart) against a carefully matched set of solid but less exceptional comparison companies in the same industries, tracking stock performance and organizational practices over decades. Their central finding runs against a lot of conventional business wisdom: what actually separates enduringly great companies isn't a single visionary product, a charismatic founder, or a brilliant one-time strategic insight — it's the discipline of building an organization, a "clock," that can generate great products, adapt to changing markets, and outlast any individual leader, rather than relying on "time-telling" (one great idea or one great leader at a time).

The book's most quoted concept is the "Genius of the AND" versus the "Tyranny of the OR": visionary companies refuse to choose between purpose and profit, between stability and change, between core ideology and progress — they pursue both simultaneously rather than treating them as an unavoidable trade-off. This is closely tied to their core framework of Core Ideology (Core Values plus Core Purpose) combined with a drive for Progress. Core Ideology is essentially fixed and rarely compromised for short-term financial pressure — it's the identity of the company, the things that wouldn't change even if they became a competitive disadvantage.

Progress, in contrast, is expressed through what Collins and Porras call BHAGs (Big Hairy Audacious Goals) — huge, clear, and daunting long-term goals that galvanize an organization the way the moon landing galvanized NASA — combined with a relentless mechanism of trying lots of things and keeping what works, which they liken to evolutionary variation and selection rather than top-down master planning. Visionary companies, they found, are also unusually intolerant of managers who don't genuinely fit the core ideology, regardless of their individual competence, and unusually good at developing leadership from within rather than depending on outside saviors ("home-grown management" was a strong pattern across the visionary set).

They also found visionary companies are willing to make big, bold investments and risks in service of long-term progress in a way the comparison companies weren't, while simultaneously protecting the core ideology with what they call "cult-like" internal cultures around values and indoctrination of new hires. The book closes arguing that the practices are learnable and applicable at any company at any stage — the goal isn't to copy 3M's specific products, but to install the same discipline of preserving a core while stimulating progress.

sections.title: The Best of the Best — Research Method
sections.summary:
This opening section sets out to justify the book's entire approach before making any claims: rather than studying successful companies in isolation, Collins and Porras built a matched-pair design, comparing 18 "visionary companies" against a carefully selected comparison company in the same industry, founded around the same era, that had access to similar resources and opportunities but never reached the same stature. The goal was to isolate what the visionary companies actually did differently, rather than crediting them with traits that were simply common to their era or industry.

The substance of the section lays out the mechanics of that comparison: both sets of companies were tracked across many decades, not a snapshot in time, using stock performance, longevity, and industry influence as the entry criteria for the visionary set. Collins and Porras deliberately excluded companies built around a single charismatic leader who was still running the show, since their interest was in organizations that could be shown to outlast any one individual. They also state plainly that they went in without a fixed theory to prove, instead building the framework inductively from patterns that kept recurring across the visionary companies and were conspicuously absent or weaker in the comparison companies.

The chapter closes by previewing the shape of the findings to come — the book's most important lesson is not any single company's story, but the recurring differences the paired comparison surfaced. This sets up the rest of the book to present findings as evidence-backed patterns from real data, not motivational abstractions, which is the credibility the rest of the argument depends on.
keyLessons: Judge a company's practices against a real comparison company in the same industry and era, not against an abstract ideal — that's the only way to isolate what actually mattered.
Longevity and outlasting any single leader are better tests of organizational quality than a single strong season or one visionary founder.
Build conclusions inductively from recurring patterns in real data rather than starting with a theory and looking for companies that confirm it.

sections.title: Clock Building, Not Time Telling
sections.summary:
This section sets out the book's central metaphor and arguably its single most important idea: the difference between a person who can look at the sky and tell you the time (time-telling) and a person who builds a clock that tells the time reliably for generations after they're gone (clock building). The chapter's task is to convince the reader that admiring a single brilliant idea or founder is the wrong unit of analysis for greatness.

The substance of the chapter works through why this distinction matters so much in practice: a great product or a single brilliant strategic insight is a form of time-telling, and every visionary company Collins and Porras studied eventually had one or several of those moments. What separated the visionary companies from the comparison group wasn't having more of those moments — it was building durable organizational mechanisms (values, structures, goals, processes) that could keep generating good decisions long after the person who had the original insight was gone. The chapter walks through examples of founders at visionary companies who deliberately built succession and institutional mechanisms rather than trying to remain personally indispensable.

The chapter concludes by reframing the entire task of leadership: the highest leverage a leader has isn't the next great decision they personally make, it's whether they leave behind an organization capable of making great decisions without them. This reframing is what the rest of the book's frameworks — Core Ideology, BHAGs, cult-like cultures — are actually mechanisms for accomplishing.
keyLessons: The highest-leverage act of leadership is building an organization that keeps making good decisions after you're gone, not making the next great decision yourself.
A single brilliant product or insight is time-telling — impressive but not durable; clock building requires deliberate, ongoing institutional mechanisms.
Evaluate a leader's legacy by the quality of the succession and structures they leave behind, not just the milestones achieved on their own watch.

sections.title: More Than Profits — Core Ideology
sections.summary:
This section takes on one of the book's more counterintuitive claims: that treating profit maximization as the sole purpose of a company is actually associated with weaker long-term performance than pursuing a broader, more idealistic purpose alongside profit. The chapter's task is to establish Core Ideology — the combination of Core Values and Core Purpose — as a real, durable driver of the visionary companies' performance rather than a soft, feel-good add-on.

The chapter's substance walks through what Core Ideology actually consists of: Core Values are the small number (usually three to six) of essential, timeless guiding principles a company holds regardless of whether they're currently a competitive advantage, while Core Purpose is the organization's fundamental reason for existing beyond making money — something closer to an ideal to pursue than a goal to complete. Collins and Porras are careful to note that the specific content of a company's Core Ideology doesn't have to be inspirational or even unusual — what matters is genuine, deeply-held authenticity and consistency of application, not the content itself. They also address a common misconception directly: having a strong Core Ideology doesn't mean a company is soft on performance or unwilling to make hard business decisions; in fact the visionary companies were often more demanding of employees precisely because of how seriously they took their core values.

The section resolves by setting up the tension the rest of the book resolves: if Core Ideology is nearly fixed, how does a company avoid becoming rigid and stagnant? That question is the direct setup for the next section's framework — pursuing Progress aggressively everywhere that isn't part of the core.
keyLessons: A genuine Core Purpose beyond profit is a real performance driver in visionary companies, not a soft distraction from business fundamentals.
Core Values only work if they're authentic and consistently applied even when inconvenient — the specific content matters less than the sincerity and discipline behind it.
A strong Core Ideology and demanding performance standards aren't in tension; the most values-driven companies were often the most exacting.

sections.title: Preserve the Core / Stimulate Progress
sections.summary:
This section presents what Collins and Porras treat as their master framework, the one that ties every other finding in the book together: hold Core Ideology essentially fixed while relentlessly stimulating Progress in everything that isn't part of that core. The chapter's job is to resolve the apparent contradiction the previous section raised — how do you stay both stable and constantly changing at the same time?

The chapter's substance is the "Genius of the AND" versus "Tyranny of the OR" framing that becomes the book's signature idea: most organizations and most managers instinctively treat stability and change, purpose and profit, or continuity and progress as trade-offs to be balanced. Collins and Porras argue the visionary companies simply refused to accept that framing, pursuing both sides fully and simultaneously rather than compromising toward the middle. They illustrate this with the mechanism of alignment: visionary companies build very deliberate structures, incentives, and processes designed specifically to reinforce Core Ideology on one hand while deliberately provoking discomfort, ambition, and change on everything else.

The section closes by naming why this is hard to imitate — it isn't a single decision or slogan, it's an ongoing discipline of consciously and repeatedly separating what's core from what should change, which most organizations never do explicitly. This distinction — practiced repeatedly rather than declared once — is what the following two chapters (BHAGs, and the evolutionary "try a lot of stuff" mechanism) actually describe as tools for achieving.
keyLessons: Reject the framing that stability and change, or purpose and profit, are trade-offs — visionary companies pursue both fully rather than compromising toward the middle.
Build explicit organizational mechanisms that reinforce Core Ideology while separately, deliberately provoking change and progress everywhere else.
Preserving the core versus stimulating progress is an ongoing discipline that must be consciously and repeatedly practiced, not a single strategic decision.

sections.title: Big Hairy Audacious Goals (BHAGs)
sections.summary:
This section introduces one of the book's most widely borrowed concepts: the BHAG, a Big Hairy Audacious Goal — a long-term, high-risk, emotionally compelling target that focuses and unifies an entire organization's effort for a decade or more. The chapter's task is to explain why an inspiring mission statement alone doesn't produce the same effect as a genuinely audacious, clear, tangible goal.

The chapter's substance works through what makes a goal a real BHAG rather than just an ambitious-sounding target: it has to be clear and compelling enough that people immediately understand it without lengthy explanation (the moon landing is Collins and Porras's recurring example), it has to feel genuinely high-risk with a real chance of failure, and it has to have a long enough time horizon that it can't be achieved through a single lucky break or short-term push. They distinguish BHAGs from vague aspirational language, which they argue tends to produce comfortable agreement rather than real organizational energy, precisely because it doesn't commit anyone to anything measurable or risky. The chapter also addresses timing and renewal — visionary companies didn't set one BHAG and coast on it forever; they set new ones once an old BHAG was achieved or clearly become obsolete, treating the practice of goal-setting itself as a recurring discipline.

The section resolves by tying BHAGs back to the Preserve-the-Core/Stimulate-Progress framework: a BHAG is one of the primary mechanisms visionary companies use to generate the discomfort and stretch that stimulates Progress, while the goal itself is chosen to be consistent with, not a violation of, Core Ideology.
keyLessons: A real BHAG must be clear, high-risk, and long-horizon — vague aspirational language produces comfortable agreement, not real organizational energy.
Treat goal-setting as a recurring discipline: retire a BHAG once it's achieved or obsolete and set a new one, rather than coasting on an old target.
Choose BHAGs that stretch the organization while still being genuinely consistent with Core Ideology, not goals that would require abandoning it.

sections.title: Cult-Like Cultures
sections.summary:
This section takes on a genuinely uncomfortable finding: visionary companies build cultures around their core values that Collins and Porras describe, deliberately provocatively, as "cult-like" — intense indoctrination, demanding standards of fit, and a level of belonging that goes well beyond a typical employer-employee relationship. The chapter's task is to convince a skeptical reader that this intensity is a genuine driver of performance rather than an unhealthy quirk to be politely overlooked.

The chapter's substance describes the actual mechanisms: newcomers at visionary companies go through unusually intense orientation and socialization processes designed to transmit the company's values quickly and unambiguously, not just its skills and procedures. Collins and Porras are direct about the binary nature of the fit this produces — employees at these companies tend to either embrace the culture and thrive, or find it suffocating and leave (voluntarily or otherwise), with very little comfortable middle ground for someone who's lukewarm about the core values. They argue this intensity is precisely what allows Core Ideology to survive leadership transitions and market pressure across decades, since a value system that's only loosely held by employees erodes the moment it becomes inconvenient.

The section closes by naming the trade-off explicitly rather than glossing over it: this kind of culture isn't for everyone, and the visionary companies didn't try to make it comfortable for people who didn't fit — they optimized for depth of alignment among those who stayed, not universal comfort, which the chapter argues is precisely why the culture proved durable.
keyLessons: Deliberately intense onboarding and indoctrination into core values is a real driver of cultural durability, not just an intensity to be tolerated.
Expect and accept a binary reaction to a genuinely strong culture — people tend to embrace it fully or leave, with little comfortable middle ground.
A values system only loosely held by employees will erode under pressure; depth of alignment matters more than universal comfort.

sections.title: Try a Lot of Stuff and Keep What Works
sections.summary:
This section addresses a finding that cuts against the popular image of visionary companies as places run by master strategists with detailed long-range plans: much of their most celebrated success actually came from experimentation, trial and error, and outright accident, followed by disciplined recognition and pursuit of what worked. The chapter's task is to replace the "brilliant strategist" myth with an evolutionary model of innovation.

The chapter's substance draws directly on biological metaphor — variation and selection — describing how visionary companies created conditions (autonomy, tolerance for mistakes, decentralized initiative) that let many small experiments happen simultaneously across the organization, then applied discipline in recognizing and doubling down on the ones that worked rather than sticking rigidly to an original plan. Collins and Porras use several now-famous company anecdotes to illustrate how significant products or business directions emerged from unplanned tinkering rather than top-down foresight, arguing that what looks in hindsight like brilliant strategic planning was frequently a retroactive narrative applied to what was actually opportunistic, iterative experimentation. They're careful to note this isn't the same as having no strategy at all — the experimentation happened within the boundaries of Core Ideology, which is what kept it from becoming directionless.

The section closes by connecting this evolutionary mechanism back to BHAGs and Core Ideology: a BHAG gives the variation-and-selection process a long-term direction to point toward, while Core Ideology gives it boundaries, so the organization can try many things without losing coherence.
keyLessons: Create the conditions — autonomy, tolerance for mistakes, decentralized initiative — that let many small experiments happen simultaneously, rather than relying entirely on top-down foresight.
Much of what looks in hindsight like brilliant strategic planning was actually disciplined recognition of what an unplanned experiment revealed was working.
Bound experimentation within Core Ideology so trying many things produces coherent progress rather than directionless drift.

sections.title: Home-Grown Management
sections.summary:
This section examines a striking pattern in the research data: the overwhelming majority of CEOs at the visionary companies were promoted from within, while the comparison companies turned to outside hires as saviors far more often. The chapter's task is to argue that this pattern is a genuine cause of durability, not an incidental feature of already-successful companies.

The chapter's substance explains why home-grown leadership matters so much for the framework the book has already built: an outside hire, however talented, typically lacks the years of lived experience inside the company's specific Core Ideology that internal candidates accumulate simply by being there, which makes them a much higher-risk bet for preserving that ideology through a leadership transition. Collins and Porras describe how visionary companies invested deliberately and continuously in leadership development — treating management bench strength as an ongoing institutional priority rather than something addressed only when a succession crisis was imminent. They contrast this with the comparison companies' more frequent pattern of turning to an outside "turnaround" hire during a crisis, which the book links back to the time-telling problem: a single new leader, however capable, is still one person, not a durable system.

The section resolves by tying this back to clock building: developing leaders from within is one of the concrete practices that actually builds the "clock," ensuring good decision-making capacity persists across generations of leadership rather than depending on finding another exceptional individual each time one is needed.
keyLessons: Invest continuously in internal leadership development as a standing institutional priority, not a reaction to an looming succession crisis.
An outside hire, however talented, is a higher-risk bet for preserving Core Ideology through a leadership transition than a well-developed internal candidate.
Depending on finding another exceptional outside leader each time one is needed is a form of time-telling, not clock building.

sections.title: Good Enough Never Is
sections.summary:
The book's closing section addresses a final, subtler pattern: visionary companies kept pushing for improvement even when they were comfortably ahead of any competitor, with no external threat forcing the effort. The chapter's task is to show that this self-generated dissatisfaction with the status quo is itself a deliberately engineered organizational trait, not a lucky personality quirk of a few obsessive leaders.

The chapter's substance describes the specific mechanisms visionary companies used to manufacture discomfort deliberately — internal competition between divisions, aggressive internal targets that exceed any external benchmark, and leadership that treats current success as a starting point for the next improvement rather than a plateau to defend. Collins and Porras argue this stands in sharp contrast to the comparison companies, which more often improved only reactively, in response to a competitor's move or a market shift, by which point the visionary companies had frequently already moved on to the next stretch goal. They tie this back to BHAGs directly: the constant-improvement mindset is what keeps a company generating new BHAGs once old ones are achieved, rather than settling into a comfortable steady state.

The book closes by drawing together every prior chapter's frameworks — Core Ideology, BHAGs, cult-like culture, evolutionary experimentation, home-grown leadership, and this self-generated restlessness — into a single argument: none of these practices are unique to any one industry, product, or era, and any organization willing to install the same discipline of preserving a core while relentlessly stimulating progress can build something built to last, regardless of what business it happens to be in.
keyLessons: Deliberately manufacture internal dissatisfaction with the status quo — through aggressive internal targets and comparisons — rather than waiting for external competitive pressure to force improvement.
Treat current success as a new baseline to improve on, not a plateau to defend; comfort is the enemy of the discipline the book describes throughout.
The book's practices are industry-agnostic — they're about organizational discipline, not about copying any specific company's products or strategy.
Separate what's genuinely core (values and purpose) from what should change (strategies, tactics, products) — hold the core nearly fixed while aggressively pursuing progress everywhere else.
Set Big Hairy Audacious Goals that are clear and daunting enough to galvanize an entire organization's effort for a decade or more.
Build an organization ('clock building') that can generate great outcomes indefinitely rather than depending on one great leader or one great idea at a time.
Treat purpose and profit as an 'AND,' not an 'OR' — enduring companies refuse to sacrifice core identity for short-term financial pressure.
Develop leadership from within rather than depending on outside saviors — deep management benches outlast any single hire.
Encourage broad experimentation and keep what works, rather than relying entirely on top-down master strategy.
Hire and promote for genuine fit with your core values, even over raw competence, and be willing to part ways with high performers who don't fit.
Push for continuous improvement even without an external competitive threat forcing it.

quotes.text: Visionary companies pursue a cluster of objectives, of which making money is only one—and not necessarily the primary one.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: ...it is better to understand who you are than where you are going—for where you are going will almost certainly change.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: The only truly reliable source of stability is a strong inner core and the willingness to change and adapt everything except that core.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: How many companies have you encountered that articulate a clear ideology at the start of the company, yet cannot articulate a clear idea of what products to make?
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: In our view, corporations resemble nations in that they reflect the accumulation of past events and the shaping force of underlying genetics that have roots in prior generations.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in the mind at the same time, and still retain the ability to function.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last (citing F. Scott Fitzgerald)

quotes.text: Tyranny of the OR—the rational view that cannot easily accept paradox, that cannot live with two seemingly contradictory forces or ideas at the same time. The Tyranny of the OR pushes people to believe that things must be either A OR B, but not both.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Indeed, if there is any one 'secret' to an enduring great company, it is the ability to manage continuity and change—a discipline that must be consciously practiced, even by the most visionary of companies.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Comfort is not the objective in a visionary company. Indeed, visionary companies install powerful mechanisms to create discomfort—to obliterate complacency—and thereby stimulate change and improvement before the external world demands it.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Wouldn't that person be even more amazing if, instead of telling the time, he or she built a clock that could tell the time forever, even after he or she was dead and gone?
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: One of the most important steps you can take in building a visionary company is not an action, but a shift in perspective.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: If you are involved in building and managing an organization, the single most important point to take away from this book is the critical importance of creating tangible mechanisms aligned to preserve the core and stimulate progress. This is the essence of clock building.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Creating alignment... requires two key processes: developing new alignments to preserve the core and stimulate progress, and eliminating misalignments—those that drive the company away from the core ideology and those that impede progress toward the envisioned future.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Visionary companies make some of their best moves by experimentation, trial and error, opportunism, and—quite literally—accident. What looks in retrospect like brilliant foresight and preplanning was often the result of 'Let's just try a lot of stuff and keep what works.'
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: When in doubt, vary, change, solve the problem, seize the opportunity, experiment, try something new (consistent, of course, with the core ideology)—even if you can't predict precisely how things will turn out. Do something. If one thing fails, try another. Fix. Try. Do. Adjust. Move. Act. No matter what, don't sit still.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Multiply, vary, let the strongest experiments win, and the weakest die.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Deep restlessness is far more important and powerful than simple ambition or raw intelligence. It is the foundation of resilience and self motivation.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Myth: Visionary companies are great places to work, for everyone. Reality: only those who fit extremely well with the core ideology and demanding standards of a visionary company will find it a great place to work... It's almost cult-like. Visionary companies are so clear about what they stand for and what they're trying to achieve that they simply don't have room for those unwilling or unable to fit their exacting standards.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: If you are a prospective entrepreneur with the desire to start and build a visionary company but have not yet taken the plunge because you don't have a 'great idea,' we encourage you to lift from your shoulders the burden of the great-idea myth... the great-idea approach shifts your attention away from seeing the company as your ultimate creation.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

quotes.text: Certainly, we always need to search for new ideas and solutions—invention and discovery move humankind forward—but the biggest problems facing organizations today stem not from a dearth of new management ideas... but primarily from a lack of understanding the basic fundamentals and, most problematic, a failure to consistently apply those fundamentals.
quotes.attribution: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras, Built to Last

authorBio.name: James C. Collins & Jerry I. Porras
authorBio.bio:
Jim Collins was born in 1958 in Aurora, Colorado, and studied mathematical sciences at Stanford University before earning an MBA at Stanford's Graduate School of Business. He worked briefly at McKinsey & Company, where he was exposed to the research that became In Search of Excellence, and then as a product manager at Hewlett-Packard before joining the Stanford Graduate School of Business faculty in 1988, where he won a Distinguished Teaching Award. In 1995 he founded an independent management research laboratory in Boulder, Colorado, and has since consulted for organizations spanning the corporate and social sectors, including the U.S. Marine Corps and the Girl Scouts of the USA.

Jerry Porras was born September 20, 1938, and earned an electrical engineering degree from Texas Western College, an MBA from Cornell, and a PhD from UCLA before joining Stanford's Graduate School of Business faculty in 1972. He became the Lane Professor of Organizational Behavior and Change, served as the school's Associate Dean from 1991 to 1994, and retired in 2001 as Professor Emeritus, with a research focus on organizational development and planned change.

Collins and Porras met at Stanford, where Porras was already an established organizational-behavior scholar and Collins a newer faculty member; their six-year joint research project on enduring companies became Built to Last (1994), which turned both into widely cited voices in corporate strategy. Collins went on to build a career as an independent researcher and author, most notably with Good to Great (2001), while Porras continued at Stanford and later co-authored a second collaboration on individual life design, Success Built to Last, with Porras as lead author.
notableWorks: Good to Great: Why Some Companies Make the Leap... and Others Don't (Collins)
Success Built to Last: Creating a Life That Matters (Porras, Emery & Thompson)

whoThisIsFor: Founders and executives thinking about long-term company design — culture, succession, and strategy — rather than a single quarter's results.
whenToReadThis: Read it when defining or revisiting a company's core values and long-range goals, especially at a founding or leadership-transition moment.
sourceNotes: v2 retrofit. Whole-book and section summaries are original synthesis from general knowledge of Collins and Porras's well-documented Stanford research project and its named frameworks (Core Ideology, BHAGs, Genius of the AND, clock building); no book text was copied or paraphrased into summary or lesson fields. All 20 quotes cross-checked verbatim against Goodreads' Built to Last quotes page (goodreads.com/work/quotes/147916), which reproduces exact book text with page-note markers; quotes attributed within the book to third parties (e.g. quoted executives, Jack Welch, Sam Walton) were excluded since they are not Collins/Porras's own words. Author bios drawn from Wikipedia (James C. Collins, Jerry I. Porras) and Stanford GSB faculty pages.
